data.title: DGA Governor: Saudi Vision 2030 Propels Kingdom into World's Leading Digital Governments
data.content:
Riyadh, November 22, 2026, SPA -- Governor of the Digital Government Authority (DGA) Eng. Ahmed bin Mohammed Alsuwaiyan affirmed that the achievements in the Kingdom's digital transformation journey result from Saudi Vision 2030, announced by His Royal Highness Prince Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, Crown Prince and Prime Minister, on April 25, 2016. This Vision is built on three main pillars: "Vibrant Society," "Thriving Economy," and "Ambitious Nation."
    Eng. Alsuwaiyan explained that the objective of "Enhancing Government Effectiveness," under the "Ambitious Nation" pillar, encompasses the goal of "Improving Government Performance." This ultimately aims to position the Kingdom among the world's top five digital governments. He noted that this ranking reflects integrated efforts primarily directed at serving citizens, residents, and visitors, while also enhancing the business environment and improving government performance efficiency.
    These remarks were made during the DGA Governor's address at the government press conference organized by the Ministry of Media in Riyadh. He highlighted the Kingdom's digital transformation journey since the launch of Saudi Vision 2030 and its ascent to an advanced ranking in the E-Government Development Index (EGDI), placing it among the world's top five digital governments.
    Eng. Alsuwaiyan pointed out that the strategic objectives of digital transformation have remained unchanged for over a decade, despite rapid technological advancements. These objectives focus on increasing productivity, improving efficiency, and enhancing the user experience. He emphasized that, during this time, the Kingdom has reached numerous significant milestones that have directly benefited individuals, government entities, and the business sector.
    Highlighting successful examples of digital transformation across government entities, he explained that the Ministry of Interior has reduced the time required to deliver numerous services via the Absher platform to just 30 seconds, down from approximately four hours. This includes services like issuing family registers and changing citizens' first names. This transformation has generated estimated annual savings of SAR26 billion and eliminated the necessity for over 1.3 million in-person visits daily, thereby simplifying procedures, improving government service efficiency, and enhancing the beneficiary experience.
    In the justice sector, the DGA Governor noted that 95% of court hearings are now conducted remotely through virtual courts. The average time required to issue judicial rulings in personal status courts has decreased from 219 days to just 20 days, eliminating the need for more than 60 million in-person visits annually.
    In healthcare, he explained that the Ministry of Health has conducted 51% of medical appointments remotely through the Seha Virtual Hospital and virtual clinics. He also highlighted the world's first use of robotic technology in surgical procedures and tumor removal at King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Center. This advancement has helped minimize surgical trauma and accelerate patient recovery, allowing patients to be discharged on the same day instead of after seven days, as was previously the case.
    Furthermore, he noted that the time required to dispense medications has been reduced to less than eight minutes, down from 72 hours previously, resulting in estimated savings of SAR1.5 billion in medication costs.
    The financial ecosystem has also developed significantly, with the share of electronic payments rising to 85%, up from 18% in 2016. Digital services now let users complete transactions on their mobile phones without carrying physical documents or payment methods, including national ID cards, driver's licenses, bank cards, or cash.
    Customs clearance time has also been reduced to just two hours, compared to 12 days in 2017, through integration with 26 government entities. Similarly, the time required to procure and supply government goods and products has dropped from 120 days to just two days, supported by a government e-marketplace offering more than 219,000 products.
    Regarding community services, the governor of the Digital Government Authority noted that the "Ehsan" platform processes more than 390,000 donations daily, with total donations reaching SAR17 billion. The time required to submit a domestic worker recruitment request has also been reduced from 30 days to just eight minutes. Meanwhile, in-person visits to Social Insurance branches and offices have been eliminated, following more than five million such visits in 2017.
    He further explained that digital transformation has improved services for pilgrims and visitors to the Two Holy Mosques. The "Nusuk" platform has surpassed 60 million users, the highest number among platforms in the Kingdom, and has the potential to expand its reach as it seeks to serve more than two billion Muslims worldwide.
    Daily visitors to Al-Rawdah Al-Sharifah have increased to 55,000, up from 4,000. The time required to issue Hajj and Umrah visas has also fallen from five days to just five minutes, with more than 22 million visas issued in 2025.
    As part of the Year of Artificial Intelligence, Eng. Alsuwaiyan said the Ministry of Energy has reduced the time to process and monitor oil and gas supplies to 30 seconds, down from 25 minutes.
    The Ministry of Municipalities and Housing has cut the cost of monitoring visual blight by 76%, from SAR197 million to SAR47 million, while expanding geographical coverage from 11% to 95%. Meanwhile, the Ministry of Environment, Water and Agriculture has achieved financial savings of approximately SAR120 million through the "Water Sustainability" platform and reduced the time required to process violations related to water resources and wells from six days to one.
    He stressed that these achievements are part of a broader range of initiatives that have delivered tangible development impact by integrating government operations and making key national enablers available.
    He also noted that the Kingdom has established a comprehensive digital government ecosystem, providing government entities with more than 20 shared resources, most notably the unified digital identity "Nafath," the government payment gateway, and the integration platform.
    More than 1,800 services are available through the unified national application "Tawakkalna," which handles over 88 million transactions daily. Meanwhile, more than 200 government entities have adopted a unified website design under the "Platforms Code" initiative.
    Highlighting the focus on placing citizens and beneficiaries at the center of government services, Alsuwaiyan said 25 integrated and interconnected service pathways, known as "life journeys," have been developed. These include services for mothers and children, as well as Hajj and Umrah pilgrims.
    He added that members of the public have contributed to government decision-making through 883 digital participation initiatives, while the digital inclusivity index, which aims to empower older adults and persons with disabilities, has reached 77%.
    To support government entities, Alsuwaiyan said an innovation center has been set up with specialized spaces, workshops, and laboratories to develop high-quality services and products.
    He noted that more than 4,000 government employees have benefited, and the center has provided more than 2,100 specialized consultations and issued more than 90 certifications in enterprise architecture and government excellence.
    Partnership with the private sector is a fundamental pillar of digital transformation, Alsuwaiyan said. He noted that government spending on information and communications technology (ICT) services exceeded SAR145 billion between 2022 and the end of last year, cloud computing adoption across government entities reached 49%, and contracts awarded to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) exceeded SAR9 billion in 2025.
    He said that national regulations and technical standards have been vital in developing digital services and improving government performance through an integrated measurement framework of four key indicators, most notably the digital transformation index, which rose from 69% in 2021 and targets 90% in 2026.
    These efforts have brought significant progress in global indices, he said.
    Alsuwaiyan stated that the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia rose from 49th place globally in 2018 to first in the world in digital government services, and Riyadh climbed from 30th in 2018 to first in the world in digital services.
    "These results mark a significant milestone in Saudi Arabia's journey toward achieving its Vision 2030 goal: to rank among the top five digital governments globally. The Kingdom has advanced in the overall E-Government Development Index from 52nd place in 2018 to 4th place globally in 2026, out of 194 countries," Alsuwaiyan said, adding that the development journey continues with growing ambition for a promising digital future.
    Responding to journalists' questions, he said all regions, governorates, centers, and villages receive equal care and attention, with high-quality digital services across the Kingdom, and that digital services have become an essential part of daily life.
    Drawing on leading global practices, the Kingdom has developed a distinctive model for using technology to serve people, reflected in services that let citizens and residents complete transactions in seconds, Alsuwaiyan added.
    On accessibility for older people and people with disabilities, and alternative channels for those facing technical difficulties, he said the authority has developed a national index based on technical standards approved by international organizations.
    He also noted that it is part of the Digital Experience Maturity Index, which evaluates more than 60 digital platforms with input from hundreds of thousands of citizens and residents.
    Alsuwaiyan stated that compliance currently stands at about 77%, with a target of 90% in cooperation with relevant entities. Development ambitions are boundless, he said, and work continues to improve service quality using modern and emerging technologies.
    On the future of government work after the Kingdom's advanced global rankings, Alsuwaiyan said e-government began by moving paper-based procedures into technical systems, before evolving into digital government, which focuses on re-engineering processes and adopting modern principles such as the once-only data submission policy and greater operational efficiency.
    He indicated that the next phase is a move toward smart government, which allows traditional operating models, including in healthcare, education, and the judiciary, to be rethought, raising efficiency and service quality.
    Moreover, Alsuwaiyan said the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) and emerging technologies extends beyond the public sector to economic sectors, automating repetitive tasks, improving job quality, and raising economic output, stressing the importance of using generative, agentic, and physical AI in logistics, transport, retail, industry, and mining to support economic growth and Saudi Arabia's competitiveness.
    Asked about consolidating digital platforms, he said platforms and websites are only tools, and the main goal is to give individuals and businesses the best possible experience. Integrating digital platforms is a cornerstone of comprehensive government, and their number has been cut from more than 800 to about 400, with a unified user experience through shared codes and components such as the unified national access system and the government payment gateway. On cybersecurity and potential attacks on digital infrastructure or data, Alsuwaiyan said digital transformation requires effective risk management, greater preparedness, and stronger digital resilience.
    The authority continuously monitors government entities' readiness and business continuity by providing alternatives, conducting periodic exercises, and running readiness tests to strengthen their capacity to deal with cyber risks. On the prospect of exporting the Kingdom's technical achievements, he said there is a very promising opportunity to share this experience and learn from others, whether by exporting technology or developing collaborative models. "Currently, every nation maintains its own independent digital government. The question is: how can we interconnect these governments to facilitate the seamless transfer of services and data, and to achieve greater efficiency? In the Kingdom, you only need your mobile phone; yet when you travel abroad, you still need to carry a physical passport. We need to engage more extensively with various organizations. Ongoing efforts are already underway—in collaboration with the United Nations, the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), and several other international bodies—to explore how we can create interconnected governments that generate value and impact, while enhancing efficiency and productivity. This requires significant work. Today, with the advent of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies, we have the potential to consistently deliver an improved experience. This is precisely what we are working toward, and, we will see some truly exceptional models emerge in the coming months," he said. "Over the past few years, we have invested in our young men and women, and we will continue to invest even more in the coming phase to ensure the best possible outcomes. Our ranking shifted from 36th to 44th, and subsequently to 52nd between 2016 and 2018. The takeaway here is that beginnings are always challenging, and one should not be hasty in expecting results. There was a significant need to restructure, organize governance, and establish the appropriate frameworks. If we look back at the Saudi Vision 2030 document, we find that an ambitious goal was set specifically for digital government," he added. Alsuwaiyan concluded: "Today, a number of government entities serve various economic sectors, with clear mechanisms and methods defined for this purpose. Despite the initial decline, the soundness of our foundational work—laying the groundwork optimally—has enabled us, to achieve our goals four years ahead of schedule and even surpass our targets. This is an achievement we take great pride in, and it stands as a testament to the success of Saudi Vision 2030."
    -- SPA
